newsitem.title: EGYPT: Syria's Assad says he wants peace.
newsitem.headline: Syria's Assad says he wants peace.

text.p: Syrian President Hafez al-Assad said in remarks published on Saturday that he was committed to peace but in no hurry to make concessions to Israel.
The Egyptian newspaper Al-Ahram also quoted Assad reiterating that Syria would not resume talks with Israel until the Jewish state evacuated from the Golan Heights.
"The Israeli position until now confirms that we are not on the road to peace, but we are committed to it despite all hostilities," the paper quoted him as saying.

Assad said he thought the U.S., co-sponsor of the peace process, wanted peace but he saw little hope because of Israel's practices. "I think the U.S. really seeks peace. But hope appears weak," Assad said. "Israel is making matters worse."
Assad, however, said he was optimistic but not in a hurry.
"I don't say this while I am depressed, on the contrary I am optimistic... But, we are not in a hurry, if such a hurry would press us to yield any of our rights," the Syrian president said.
Syria and Israel held five years of sporadic talks over the Golan Heights, occupied by the Jewish state since the 1967 war.
They have yet to resume since right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government took over in June.
"We truly want peace. We want it for all. We don't want to drown in other arrangements.." Assad said. "I have once said that land is not for bargaining and that peace is for all.

Syria, demanding the return of the heights, has assailed Netanyahu for rejecting the land-for-peace policy of the left-leaning government he ousted in May and for backing Jewish settlement on the plateau.
Netanyahu vowed on Wednesday he would make the peace with Syria that evaded his Israeli predecessors, despite his refusal to give up the occupied Golan Heights.

He also repeated his prediction of a peace deal with Syria by the end of his first term in the year 2000 but demanded that Syria stop guerrilla attacks against Israel from Lebanon, where Damascus is the main power broker with 30,000 troops.

Al-Ahram quoted Assad as saying that there were no continuous contacts between Syria and Israel since Netanyahu came to power, and that there would be none unless they were based on what had been agreed.
